sections.title: Introduction & Basic Definition
sections.content: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a degenerative disorder in which the structure and function of the macula deteriorates. It is characterized by the presence of specific clinical findings, including drusen and RPE changes, in the absence of another disorder. Later stages of the disease are associated with impairment of vision secondary to neovascularization or atrophy.

headers: Definition (Presence of lesions within two disc diameters of the fovea)
rows: No drusen; No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Only drupelets; No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Medium drusen (>63 μm but <125 μm); No AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Large drusen (>125 μm); Any AMD pigmentary abnormalities
Neovascular AMD and/or Any geographic atrophy

sections.title: Nomenclature & Main Types
content: A consensus committee provided the clinical classification and standardized nomenclature for neovascular AMD.
Dry (non-exudative, non-neovascular) AMD: Most common form (90%). Geographic atrophy (GA) is the advanced stage. Note: It's suggested 'dry AMD' should describe GA rather than early stages.
Wet (exudative, neovascular) AMD: Less common but rapid progression to sight loss. Main entities: MNV, PED, RAP, and PCV.
TIP: The term 'choroidal neovascularization' (CNV) is no longer appropriate because neovascularization may start in the outer retina. Macular neovascularization (MNV) should be used instead.

sections.title: Epidemiological Context
content: Most common cause of irreversible visual loss in industrialized countries.
In USA: Severe sight loss = better eye worse than 6/60.
Symptoms rare in patients under 50 years of age.
UK: 1.6% of those over 75 have binocular acuity of less than 6/60.
Fellow Eye Risk: Patients with late AMD in one eye (or moderate loss in non-advanced AMD) have a 50% chance of developing advanced AMD in the fellow eye within 5 years.

branches: Genetic Susceptibility (CFH gene 1q31 - 7x risk; ARMS2 gene 10q26 - 8x risk)
Aspirin (Weak statistical association; benefits outweigh risk)
Other factors (Cataract surgery, Blue iris, Sunlight, Female gender)

sections.title: Drusen: Histopathology
sections.content: Drusen are extracellular deposits located at the interface between the RPE and Bruch membrane. Composed of constituents from immune-mediated and metabolic processes in the RPE. Role in pathogenesis is unclear but associated with lesion size and pigmentary abnormalities. Rare before age 40; common by the sixth decade. Distribution: Variable (fovea, encircling fovea, band around macular periphery, or mid-peripheral fundus).

sections.title: Drusen: Clinical Features & Sizes
content: Small Drusen (Drupelets): ≤63 μm (half width of retinal vein at disc). Well-defined, white-yellow. Little visual loss risk alone.
Intermediate Drusen: 63–125 μm. Yellow-white focal deposits. <10% 5-year progression risk unless bilateral pigmentary changes present (>10%).
Large Drusen ('Soft'): >125 μm. Less well delineated. May coalesce into 'drusenoid RPE detachment'. 13% bilateral progression risk; 50% with bilateral pigmentary changes.
Dystrophic Calcification: May develop in all types.
Pigmentary Abnormalities: Hyper- and hypopigmentation (not due to other disease) significantly increases visual loss risk.

branches: Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (malattia leventinese): Autosomal dominant radial drusen; appears 2nd-3rd decades.
Cuticular drusen (Basal laminar drusen): Small (25–75 μm) yellowish nodules; clustering; FA shows 'stars in the sky'; linked to CFH variant.
Type 2 membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Chronic renal disease; bilateral diffuse drusen-like lesions; CFH gene implicated.

sections.title: Drusen Imaging & Diagnostic Tools
content: TIP: Strong association between risk of advanced AMD, drusen size, and macular pigmentary change.
Size Estimation: Retinal vein diameter at optic disc margin is approx 125 μm.
OCT: Medium/Large drusen seen as hyper-reflective irregular nodules beneath RPE, on or within Bruch membrane.
FA: Hyperfluorescence (window defect from atrophy or late staining). Hypofluorescence (hydrophobic, high lipid content masking fluorescence).

sections.title: Antioxidant Supplementation (AREDS)
content: AREDS1/AREDS2 Evidence: High-dose antioxidants/minerals decrease risk of advanced AMD.
Recommendation (Age >55 with high-risk signs): Extensive intermediate drusen, One or more large drusen, GA in one or both eyes, or Late AMD in one eye.
Risk Reduction: 25–30% reduction in 10-year progression risk for advanced baseline signs. No reduction seen in early or no AMD.
AREDS1 Regimen: Vitamin C, E, Beta-carotene, Zinc (80mg), Copper.

content.explanation: Vitamin E (400 IU), Vitamin C (500 mg), Lutein (10 mg), Zeaxanthin (2 mg), Zinc (25–80 mg; lower may be equally effective), Copper (2 mg; not required with low-dose zinc).

sections.title: AREDS2 Key Findings
content: Lutein/Zeaxanthin: Safe and superior alternative to Beta-carotene (18% risk reduction).
Beta-carotene Warning: Increases lung cancer incidence in current/former smokers.
Zinc: 25 mg is maximal absorbed; lower dose reduces genitourinary/GI side effects.
Omega-3: Adding omega-3 fatty acids did not enhance outcomes.
Competition: Carotenoids may compete for absorption.
Cataract Benefit: One-third reduction in likelihood of cataract surgery in specific groups.

sections.title: Lifestyle Considerations
content: Green leafy vegetables: Lower risk (prudent for family history/early AMD).
Smoking cessation: Strongly advised.
Sun protection: Consider protective measures.
Oily fish: Consumption supported by some authorities.
TIP: Regular antioxidant dietary supplementation can reduce advanced AMD risk in high-risk dry AMD patients.

sections.title: Non-Exudative (Dry) AMD Overview
sections.content: A common condition threatening vision in up to 5 million people worldwide. Loss of photoreceptors and RPE cells results in Geographic Atrophy (GA). Process is slow but GA results in significant acuity loss and is an inevitable long-term outcome for many wet AMD patients. Lesion size is measured by FAF. Pathogenesis involves complement factors C3 and C5 activation.

sections.title: Dry AMD Diagnosis & Symptoms
content: Symptoms: Gradual vision impairment (months/years); usually bilateral but asymmetric. Vision fluctuates and may be better in bright light.

Sign Sequence: 1. Numerous intermediate-large soft drusen (may coalesce). 2. Focal hyper- or hypopigmentation. 3. Circumscribed RPE atrophy (loss of retina/choriocapillaris). 4. Geographic Atrophy (GA) with visible larger choroidal vessels and disappearing drusen. 5. Drusenoid RPE detachment.

sections.title: Advanced Imaging for Dry AMD
content: OCT: Loss of RPE and morphologic retinal alterations. Increased hyper-reflectivity in outer layers.
Outer Retinal Tubulations (OCT): Roundish hyporeflective spaces (degenerating photoreceptors) often at GA margins.
Outer Retinal Corrugations (OCT): Undulating hyper-reflective layer; Histological Basal Laminar Deposit (between RPE and basement membrane).
Basal Linear Deposit: Membranous debris between RPE basement membrane and Bruch membrane (may form drusen).
Microperimetry: Accurate method of testing central vision.
FAF: Visualizes atrophy; Hyperautofluorescence in junctional zone indicates higher progression risk.
FA: Window defect due to unmasked background fluorescence (if choriocapillaris intact); scleral late staining.

sections.title: Management of Dry AMD
content: 1. Prophylaxis: AREDS supplementation + address risk factors (smoking, sun, CV, diet).
2. Home Monitoring: Provide Amsler grid with advice for regular self-testing.
3. Visual Support: Provision of low vision aids and visually impaired certification.
4. Future: Complement inhibitors (Avacincaptad pegol [C5] or Pegcetacoplan [C3]) reduce GA growth in short term.

sections.title: Ineffective or Experimental Treatments
content: Emixustat (Visual cycle modulation): Not helpful in slowing atrophy growth.
Photocoagulation of drusen: Reduces extent but does not reduce progression risk.
Saffron (20 mg/day): Short-term improvement in retinal function.

Experimental Surgery: Miniature intraocular telescope; RPE stem cell implants (improved vision in some); Macular translocation (unsuccessful/high complication rate); Visual prostheses (under investigation).
